{"questions": [
{"id": "p1", "topic": "combinatorics: subsets (counting 2-element subsets, factor pairs)", "error_type": "omitted_case",
"question": "Find the sum of the positive integers m for which there exists a positive integer n < m such that the number of 2-element subsets of an m-element set exceeds the number of 2-element subsets of an n-element set by exactly 315.",
"answer": 942, "target_wrong": 912,
"error_description": "The factor pair 14·45 of 630 is left out of the list of factorizations; it gives m − n = 14, m + n − 1 = 45, i.e. (m, n) = (30, 16), so the sum loses 30.",
"cases": ["1·630 → m=316", "2·315 → m=159", "3·210 → m=107", "5·126 → m=66", "6·105 → m=56", "7·90 → m=49", "9·70 → m=40", "10·63 → m=37", "14·45 → m=30", "15·42 → m=29", "18·35 → m=27", "21·30 → m=26"],
"solution": "We need C(m,2) − C(n,2) = 315, i.e. m(m−1) − n(n−1) = 630, which factors as (m−n)(m+n−1) = 630. Put d = m−n and e = m+n−1. Since n ≥ 1, e − d = 2n − 1 ≥ 1, so d < e, and d + e = 2m − 1 is odd, so d and e have opposite parity. Because 630 = 2·3²·5·7 has exactly one factor of 2, every factorization 630 = d·e with d < e automatically has opposite parity, so every such factor pair works. The pairs (d, e) are (1,630), (2,315), (3,210), (5,126), (6,105), (7,90), (9,70), (10,63), (14,45), (15,42), (18,35), (21,30). From m = (d+e+1)/2 the values of m are 316, 159, 107, 66, 56, 49, 40, 37, 30, 29, 27, 26, and the corresponding n = (e−d+1)/2 are 315, 157, 104, 61, 50, 42, 31, 27, 16, 14, 9, 5, all positive and less than m. The twelve values of m are distinct, and their sum is 316+159+107+66+56+49+40+37+30+29+27+26 = 942.",
"check_code": "ms=set()\nfor m in range(2,2000):\n    cm=m*(m-1)//2\n    for n in range(1,m):\n        if cm-n*(n-1)//2==315:\n            ms.add(m)\nprint(sum(ms))"},

{"id": "p2", "topic": "combinatorics: subsets (3-element subsets forming geometric progressions)", "error_type": "omitted_case",
"question": "How many 3-element subsets of {1, 2, 3, …, 40} have the property that their elements can be arranged to form a geometric progression? (The common ratio need not be an integer.)",
"answer": 28, "target_wrong": 27,
"error_description": "The ratio 6/5 case is omitted: the progression 25, 30, 36 (from kq² = 25, kpq = 30, kp² = 36 with k = 1, p = 6, q = 5) is missed, so the count is 27 instead of 28.",
"cases": ["ratio 2: a·{1,2,4}, a ≤ 10 → 10 sets", "ratio 3: a·{1,3,9}, a ≤ 4 → 4 sets", "ratio 3/2: a·{4,6,9}, a ≤ 4 → 4 sets", "ratio 4: a·{1,4,16}, a ≤ 2 → 2 sets", "ratio 4/3: a·{9,12,16}, a ≤ 2 → 2 sets", "ratio 5: {1,5,25} → 1 set", "ratio 5/2: {4,10,25} → 1 set", "ratio 5/3: {9,15,25} → 1 set", "ratio 5/4: {16,20,25} → 1 set", "ratio 6: {1,6,36} → 1 set", "ratio 6/5: {25,30,36} → 1 set"],
"solution": "Write the progression as a < ar < ar² with rational ratio r = p/q > 1 in lowest terms. For ar² = ap²/q² to be an integer with gcd(p,q) = 1 we need q² | a, so a = kq² and the three terms are kq², kpq, kp² for a positive integer k. The constraint is kp² ≤ 40, so p ≤ 6. For each coprime pair (p, q) with p > q ≥ 1 the number of valid k is ⌊40/p²⌋: p = 2: q = 1 gives 10; p = 3: q = 1, 2 give 4 each (8); p = 4: q = 1, 3 give 2 each (4); p = 5: q = 1, 2, 3, 4 give 1 each (4); p = 6: q = 1, 5 give 1 each (2). Total 10 + 8 + 4 + 4 + 2 = 28. Distinct (p, q, k) give distinct sets since the set determines the ratio and the smallest term.",
"check_code": "from itertools import combinations\nc=0\nfor a,b,d in combinations(range(1,41),3):\n    if b*b==a*d:\n        c+=1\nprint(c)"},

{"id": "p3", "topic": "combinatorics: selections (collinear triples of lattice points)", "error_type": "omitted_case",
"question": "Consider the 25 points (x, y) with x and y integers satisfying 0 ≤ x ≤ 4 and 0 ≤ y ≤ 4. How many 3-element subsets of these 25 points consist of three collinear points?",
"answer": 152, "target_wrong": 140,
"error_description": "The lines of slope ±2 and ±1/2 (such as (0,0),(1,2),(2,4)) are omitted; there are 3 such lines in each of the four directions, each containing exactly 3 grid points, so 12 collinear triples are missed.",
"cases": ["rows: 5·C(5,3) = 50", "columns: 5·C(5,3) = 50", "slope 1 main diagonal (5 points): 10", "slope 1 diagonals with 4 points: 2·C(4,3) = 8", "slope 1 diagonals with 3 points: 2·1 = 2", "slope −1 main diagonal: 10", "slope −1 diagonals with 4 points: 8", "slope −1 diagonals with 3 points: 2", "lines of slope ±2 and ±1/2 (3 points each): 4·3 = 12"],
"solution": "A line containing k of the grid points contributes C(k,3) collinear triples, so we classify the lines through at least 3 grid points. Horizontal lines: 5 lines of 5 points, 5·10 = 50. Vertical lines: 50. Slope 1: the main diagonal has 5 points (10 triples), the two diagonals next to it have 4 points (4 each, total 8), and the two after that have 3 points (1 each, total 2): 20 in all. Slope −1 by symmetry: 20. Slope 2: a line y = 2x + c contains grid points with x-values differing by 1 and y-values differing by 2; three such points need a y-range of 4, so the lines are {(0,0),(1,2),(2,4)}, {(1,0),(2,2),(3,4)}, {(2,0),(3,2),(4,4)}: 3 triples. By symmetry slope −2, slope 1/2 and slope −1/2 give 3 each, for 12. Any other slope (e.g. 3, 3/2, 1/3) would need a coordinate range of at least 6 for three points, impossible in a range of 4. Total 50 + 50 + 20 + 20 + 12 = 152.",
"check_code": "from itertools import combinations\npts=[(x,y) for x in range(5) for y in range(5)]\nc=0\nfor (x1,y1),(x2,y2),(x3,y3) in combinations(pts,3):\n    if (x2-x1)*(y3-y1)==(x3-x1)*(y2-y1):\n        c+=1\nprint(c)"},

{"id": "p4", "topic": "combinatorics: set partitions (partitions with no singleton blocks)", "error_type": "omitted_case",
"question": "Nine students are to be divided into study groups so that every group has at least two students. The number of groups is not fixed in advance, and the groups are not labeled. In how many ways can this be done?",
"answer": 3425, "target_wrong": 3047,
"error_description": "The group-size pattern 5+2+2 is left out of the list of ways to write 9 as a sum of parts ≥ 2; it contributes C(9,5)·C(4,2)/2 = 378 partitions.",
"cases": ["9: 1", "7+2: C(9,2) = 36", "6+3: C(9,3) = 84", "5+4: C(9,4) = 126", "5+2+2: C(9,5)·C(4,2)/2 = 378", "4+3+2: C(9,4)·C(5,3) = 1260", "3+3+3: 9!/(3!³·3!) = 280", "3+2+2+2: C(9,3)·6!/(2!³·3!) = 1260"],
"solution": "We count set partitions of a 9-element set with every block of size at least 2, organised by the multiset of block sizes, i.e. by partitions of 9 into parts ≥ 2: 9, 7+2, 6+3, 5+4, 5+2+2, 4+3+2, 3+3+3, 3+2+2+2. For a size pattern with blocks of sizes s₁,…,s_r in which a size appears c times, the number of set partitions is 9!/(∏ sᵢ! · ∏ c!). This gives: 9 → 1; 7+2 → C(9,2) = 36; 6+3 → C(9,3) = 84; 5+4 → C(9,4) = 126; 5+2+2 → C(9,5)·(C(4,2)/2) = 126·3 = 378; 4+3+2 → C(9,4)·C(5,3) = 126·10 = 1260; 3+3+3 → 9!/(6³·6) = 280; 3+2+2+2 → C(9,3)·(6!/(2!³·3!)) = 84·15 = 1260. Summing: 1 + 36 + 84 + 126 + 378 + 1260 + 280 + 1260 = 3425.",
"check_code": "def parts(n):\n    if n==0:\n        yield []\n        return\n    for p in parts(n-1):\n        for i in range(len(p)):\n            yield p[:i]+[p[i]+1]+p[i+1:]\n        yield p+[1]\nprint(sum(1 for p in parts(9) if min(p)>=2))"},

{"id": "p5", "topic": "combinatorics: subsets (3-element subsets with sum divisible by 5, residue classes)", "error_type": "omitted_case",
"question": "How many 3-element subsets of {1, 2, 3, …, 33} have the property that the sum of their elements is divisible by 5?",
"answer": 1091, "target_wrong": 1071,
"error_description": "The residue pattern {0,0,0} (three elements all divisible by 5) is omitted from the list of residue multisets summing to 0 mod 5; it contributes C(6,3) = 20 subsets.",
"cases": ["residues {0,0,0}: C(6,3) = 20", "residues {1,1,3}: C(7,2)·7 = 147", "residues {2,2,1}: C(7,2)·7 = 147", "residues {3,3,4}: C(7,2)·6 = 126", "residues {4,4,2}: C(6,2)·7 = 105", "residues {0,1,4}: 6·7·6 = 252", "residues {0,2,3}: 6·7·7 = 294"],
"solution": "Among 1, …, 33 the residues mod 5 occur with multiplicities: residue 1: 7 numbers (1,6,…,31); residue 2: 7 (2,…,32); residue 3: 7 (3,…,33); residue 4: 6 (4,…,29); residue 0: 6 (5,…,30). A 3-element subset has sum ≡ 0 mod 5 exactly when the multiset of its residues is one of: all equal — {0,0,0} (3a ≡ 0 forces a ≡ 0); two equal and one different — {a,a,b} with b ≡ −2a ≠ a, giving {1,1,3}, {2,2,1}, {3,3,4}, {4,4,2}; all distinct — among the 10 triples of distinct residues only {0,1,4} and {0,2,3} sum to 0 mod 5. Counting subsets: {0,0,0}: C(6,3) = 20; {1,1,3}: C(7,2)·7 = 147; {2,2,1}: C(7,2)·7 = 147; {3,3,4}: C(7,2)·6 = 126; {4,4,2}: C(6,2)·7 = 105; {0,1,4}: 6·7·6 = 252; {0,2,3}: 6·7·7 = 294. Total 20 + 147 + 147 + 126 + 105 + 252 + 294 = 1091.",
"check_code": "from itertools import combinations\nprint(sum(1 for s in combinations(range(1,34),3) if sum(s)%5==0))"},

{"id": "p6", "topic": "combinatorics: selections (pairs with square sum)", "error_type": "omitted_case",
"question": "How many 2-element subsets {a, b} of {1, 2, 3, …, 60} have the property that a + b is a perfect square?",
"answer": 123, "target_wrong": 113,
"error_description": "The square 100 is omitted from the list of attainable square sums (the solver stops at 81 even though sums go up to 119); the pairs (40,60), (41,59), …, (49,51) contribute 10 subsets.",
"cases": ["sum 4: 1 pair", "sum 9: 4 pairs", "sum 16: 7 pairs", "sum 25: 12 pairs", "sum 36: 17 pairs", "sum 49: 24 pairs", "sum 64: a from 4 to 31, 28 pairs", "sum 81: a from 21 to 40, 20 pairs", "sum 100: a from 40 to 49, 10 pairs"],
"solution": "The sum of two distinct elements ranges from 3 to 119, so the possible square sums are 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100. For a sum s, pairs a < b with a + b = s and b ≤ 60 correspond to a with max(1, s − 60) ≤ a ≤ ⌊(s−1)/2⌋. For s ≤ 61 the lower bound is 1 and the count is ⌊(s−1)/2⌋: s = 4 → 1, 9 → 4, 16 → 7, 25 → 12, 36 → 17, 49 → 24. For s = 64: a from 4 to 31, 28 pairs. For s = 81: a from 21 to 40, 20 pairs. For s = 100: a from 40 to 49, 10 pairs. Total 1 + 4 + 7 + 12 + 17 + 24 + 28 + 20 + 10 = 123.",
"check_code": "from math import isqrt\nc=0\nfor a in range(1,61):\n    for b in range(a+1,61):\n        s=a+b\n        if isqrt(s)**2==s:\n            c+=1\nprint(c)"},

{"id": "p7", "topic": "combinatorics: subsets (counting subsets by size, quadratic equation)", "error_type": "algebra_slip",
"question": "A set S has n elements. The number of 2-element subsets of S is 169 more than the number of subsets of S that have at most one element. Find n.",
"answer": 20, "target_wrong": 17,
"error_description": "In solving n² − 3n − 340 = 0 the sign of the linear coefficient is flipped in the quadratic formula (or the factorization is written as (n + 20)(n − 17)), giving n = (−3 + 37)/2 = 17 instead of (3 + 37)/2 = 20.",
"cases": [],
"solution": "The number of 2-element subsets is C(n,2) = n(n−1)/2, and the number of subsets with at most one element is 1 + n (the empty set and the n singletons). The condition is n(n−1)/2 − (n + 1) = 169. Multiplying by 2: n² − n − 2n − 2 = 338, so n² − 3n − 340 = 0, which factors as (n − 20)(n + 17) = 0. Since n is positive, n = 20. Check: C(20,2) = 190 and 1 + 20 = 21, and 190 − 21 = 169.",
"check_code": "for n in range(1,10000):\n    if n*(n-1)//2-(1+n)==169:\n        print(n)\n        break"},

{"id": "p8", "topic": "combinatorics: subsets (subsets with a parity constraint)", "error_type": "misread_condition",
"question": "How many 7-element subsets of {1, 2, 3, …, 16} contain at least five even numbers?",
"answer": 1800, "target_wrong": 1568,
"error_description": "The condition 'at least five even numbers' is read as 'exactly five even numbers', giving only the term C(8,5)·C(8,2) = 1568 and dropping the cases with six or seven even numbers (224 + 8).",
"cases": [],
"solution": "The set {1,…,16} has 8 even numbers and 8 odd numbers. A 7-element subset with exactly k even numbers can be chosen in C(8,k)·C(8,7−k) ways. We need k = 5, 6, or 7: k = 5: C(8,5)·C(8,2) = 56·28 = 1568; k = 6: C(8,6)·C(8,1) = 28·8 = 224; k = 7: C(8,7)·C(8,0) = 8. Total 1568 + 224 + 8 = 1800.",
"check_code": "from itertools import combinations\nprint(sum(1 for s in combinations(range(1,17),7) if sum(1 for x in s if x%2==0)>=5))"},

{"id": "p9", "topic": "combinatorics: subsets (inclusion-exclusion on divisibility conditions)", "error_type": "double_counting",
"question": "How many 4-element subsets of {1, 2, 3, …, 12} contain at least one multiple of 3 and at least one multiple of 4?",
"answer": 314, "target_wrong": 299,
"error_description": "In the complement count, the subsets containing no multiple of 3 and the subsets containing no multiple of 4 are both subtracted from the total, but the 15 subsets containing neither (4-element subsets of {1,2,5,7,10,11}) are not added back, so they are removed twice: 495 − 70 − 126 = 299.",
"cases": [],
"solution": "The multiples of 3 in {1,…,12} are 3, 6, 9, 12 and the multiples of 4 are 4, 8, 12 (12 is both). There are C(12,4) = 495 subsets in total. Let A be the set of 4-element subsets with no multiple of 3: these are chosen from the other 8 numbers, |A| = C(8,4) = 70. Let B be those with no multiple of 4: chosen from the other 9 numbers, |B| = C(9,4) = 126. A ∩ B consists of subsets avoiding {3,4,6,8,9,12}, i.e. chosen from the 6 numbers {1,2,5,7,10,11}: |A ∩ B| = C(6,4) = 15. By inclusion-exclusion, the number of subsets with at least one multiple of 3 and at least one multiple of 4 is 495 − |A ∪ B| = 495 − (70 + 126 − 15) = 495 − 181 = 314.",
"check_code": "from itertools import combinations\nprint(sum(1 for s in combinations(range(1,13),4) if any(x%3==0 for x in s) and any(x%4==0 for x in s)))"},

{"id": "p10", "topic": "combinatorics: selections (pairs with a lower bound on their difference)", "error_type": "off_by_one",
"question": "How many 2-element subsets {a, b} of {1, 2, 3, …, 40} satisfy |a − b| ≥ 7?",
"answer": 561, "target_wrong": 528,
"error_description": "The boundary difference 7 is handled as if the condition were |a − b| > 7: the pairs with difference exactly 7 (there are 33 of them) are excluded, e.g. by subtracting the pairs with difference at most 7 instead of at most 6 from the total, giving 780 − 252 = 528.",
"cases": [],
"solution": "For a fixed difference d with 1 ≤ d ≤ 39, the pairs {a, a + d} with 1 ≤ a and a + d ≤ 40 number 40 − d. We need d ≥ 7, so the count is Σ_{d=7}^{39} (40 − d) = 33 + 32 + … + 1 = 33·34/2 = 561. Equivalently, of the C(40,2) = 780 pairs, those with difference at most 6 number 39 + 38 + 37 + 36 + 35 + 34 = 219, and 780 − 219 = 561.",
"check_code": "from itertools import combinations\nprint(sum(1 for a,b in combinations(range(1,41),2) if b-a>=7))"}
]}
